focus: Section 3, Algorithm 1 (Batch Normalizing Transform). Explain how a mini-batch of activations is normalized using the batch mean and variance and then scaled and shifted by learnable gamma and beta. Let the learner edit a small mini-batch and change gamma, beta and epsilon. Show the batch mean, variance, normalized values and outputs. Guide them through a batch with an outlier and a batch of identical values. Check that normalized values have mean 0 and (with epsilon = 0) variance 1, and that gamma = sqrt(var + eps), beta = mean recovers the input.
audience: engineering undergraduate who knows what a neural network layer is
excerpt: Section 3, Normalization via Mini-Batch Statistics (paraphrased). Consider a mini-batch B of size m of the values of one activation, B = {x1...xm}. The Batch Normalizing Transform BN_{gamma,beta}: x1...xm -> y1...ym is given in Algorithm 1: mini-batch mean mu_B = (1/m) sum_i x_i; mini-batch variance sigma_B^2 = (1/m) sum_i (x_i - mu_B)^2; normalize x_hat_i = (x_i - mu_B) / sqrt(sigma_B^2 + epsilon); scale and shift y_i = gamma * x_hat_i + beta. Epsilon is a constant added to the mini-batch variance for numerical stability. Simply normalizing each input of a layer may change what the layer can represent. To address this, the transformation inserted in the network can represent the identity transform: for each activation, a pair of parameters gamma and beta scale and shift the normalized value. These parameters are learned along with the original model parameters and restore the representation power of the network. Indeed, by setting gamma = sqrt(Var[x]) and beta = E[x], we could recover the original activations, if that were the optimal thing to do.
